description:
Ares Sentinel : La carte intelligente qui aide les premiers astronautes à décider si une sortie sur Mars est sûre.

Ares est le nom grec associé à Mars et Sentinel  évoque un gardien, une vigie, un système de surveillance et d'alerte.
summary: Ares Sentinel is an AI-powered explorer of NASA’s Curiosity weather data. It combines two AI layers on the REMS temperature and pressure archive (Gale Crater, 4,745 sols). First, machine learning: an Isolation Forest model (scikit-learn) analyzes four measurements at once and flags about 3% of days, 142 anomalies, explaining which measurement is furthest from typical values. Second, a large language model, accessed through OpenRouter, powers an AI science assistant that answers in a “Finding → Evidence → Limits” format. The LLM only receives evidence computed locally from NASA data, and a number checker flags any figure it cannot verify. Around these two AI engines, a dashboard shows an educational 0–100 verdict, a Mars map (NASA Mars Trek) and the factors behind each score for any sol or Earth date. It is an educational tool, not a NASA safety threshold.
details:
AI at the core. Ares Sentinel uses two forms of artificial intelligence. Machine learning: an Isolation Forest (scikit-learn), an unsupervised anomaly detection algorithm, scans four measurements per day (minimum temperature, maximum temperature, daily swing, pressure) and flags the 142 most unusual days (about 3%), with a robust z-score naming the measurement that makes each one unusual. A large language model, accessed through OpenRouter (OpenAI-compatible SDK), powers the AI science assistant, which answers questions about any sol in a Finding → Evidence → Limits format.

Grounded, verifiable AI. The LLM never invents data. The backend first computes evidence locally from the NASA dataset (selected sol, global statistics, leading anomalies, season comparison), then sends one request to OpenRouter. A number checker compares the figures in the answer with the local results and flags any it cannot find. Without an API key, or if the provider fails, the API returns an explicit error rather than a fabricated answer.

What it does. The app turns the Curiosity REMS archive (4,745 sols, August 2012 – August 2026) into a sol/date dashboard, a Mars map, a clickable index history, an ML anomaly explorer and the AI assistant. The educational index is 0.35 × cold + 0.25 × swing + 0.20 × pressure + 0.20 × anomaly, where each factor is a rank over the full history. A first version with fixed thresholds put 98% of days in orange, hence the rank-based design.

Integrity. Missing values are never invented: 28 days without measurements stay “unknown”. Only Gale Crater has real data.

Impact. To make Martian weather understandable for students and the public through transparent AI. The index is educational and relative to Curiosity’s own history, not a NASA safety threshold.

Tools. Python, FastAPI, Uvicorn, Pydantic, pandas, NumPy, scikit-learn (Isolation Forest), OpenRouter (LLM), JavaScript, HTML5, CSS3, Leaflet, pytest, uv, Git/GitHub, Render.

Next steps. A real Jezero verdict with Perseverance (MEDA), a 3D globe, next-day index prediction, conversation memory and streaming answers.

Team. Fidèle Miakanda (project lead, Computer and AI Engineering), Joseph Kishimba (Electromechanical Engineering), Exaucé Yewe (Electrical and Computer Engineering).
